packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts vs apps/web/components/dialog/AddGuestsDialog.tsx — two differently-shaped schemas share the name `ZAddGuestsInputSchema`; the server one (the real security boundary) has no uniqueness refine, only the client copy does (confidence=100, P2).

adjudication.rationale: Yes. The diff introduces two different `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` definitions: a client-local constant in `AddGuestsDialog.tsx` that refines for unique emails, and the server-side `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts` which only validates `guests` as `z.array(z.string().email())` with no uniqueness constraint. Since the TRPC procedure uses the server schema as the real validation boundary, a caller can bypass the client refine and submit duplicates. The handler’s `uniqueGuests` filter only excludes existing attendees/blacklisted emails and does not dedupe duplicates within the input, so duplicates can flow into `createMany` and potentially create duplicate attendee records / redundant downstream processing. The naming collision also increases the risk of assuming server-side uniqueness enforcement when it doesn’t exist.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:26-42,92-106 — read-then-write with no transaction/unique constraint; concurrent addGuests calls for the same booking+email can both pass the dedup check and both insert (TOCTOU) (confidence=85, P2).

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the code first reads the booking including current attendees (findFirst include attendees), then computes `uniqueGuests` by checking against that in-memory attendee list, and finally performs a separate `booking.update` with `attendees.createMany`. There is no transaction tying the read to the write, and `createMany` is used without `skipDuplicates`. Two concurrent requests for the same booking with the same guest email can both observe the email as absent and then both attempt to insert it. Depending on whether a DB unique constraint exists (not shown in this diff), this can result in duplicated attendees or a unique-constraint error; either way the read-then-write dedup is not concurrency-safe as implemented.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:168 vs 74-90 — `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` uses the raw unfiltered `guests` list (not `uniqueGuests`), so a resubmitted already-existing attendee is misclassified as "new" and sent the wrong email template (confidence=90, P1).

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts, the handler computes `uniqueGuests` by filtering out emails that already exist in `booking.attendees` and blacklisted emails, and only those `uniqueGuests` are actually added via `createMany`. However, it later calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` with the original unfiltered `guests` input. In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, attendees are classified based on whether their email is included in the `newGuests` array (`newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`). If the client submits a mix of already-existing attendee emails plus at least one truly new guest, `uniqueGuests.length > 0` so the mutation succeeds, but the already-existing attendees are still present in `evt.attendees` and will be misclassified as “new” because they appear in the raw `guests` list. This is a concrete, verifiable correctness bug introduced by passing `guests` instead of `uniqueGuests`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:70-72 — `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` parsed ad hoc inline with no whitespace trimming, so `"a@x.com, b@x.com"` yields a leading-space entry that never matches (confidence=95, P3).

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the blacklist is built as `process.env.BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS.split(",").map((email) => email.toLowerCase())` with no `.trim()`. Therefore an env value like `"a@x.com, b@x.com"` produces a second entry of `" b@x.com"` (leading space), and the later check `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` will not match `"b@x.com"`. This is a real correctness bug introduced in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:124-147 vs packages/emails/email-manager.ts:531-537 — `evt.team` is never populated by the handler, so the team-member notification branch is dead code and co-hosts never get notified (confidence=85, P1).

adjudication.rationale: The handler builds `evt: CalendarEvent` with fields like `organizer`, `attendees`, `destinationCalendar`, etc., but never sets `evt.team` (see addGuests.handler.ts around the `const evt: CalendarEvent = { ... }` block). In `sendAddGuestsEmails`, the team-member notification loop is guarded by `if (calendarEvent.team?.members) { ... }`, so with no `team` populated on the event, that branch will never execute. adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:46-48 — the `&&`/`||` bug denies a valid caller role (plain team admin who isn't organizer/attendee) (confidence=75, P1).

adjudication.rationale:
In addGuests.handler.ts the permission flag is computed as:

```ts
const isTeamAdminOrOwner =
  (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) &&
  (await isTeamOwner(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0));
```

Despite the variable name "isTeamAdminOrOwner", this requires the user to be BOTH an admin AND an owner. The subsequent check:

```ts
if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw FORBIDDEN;
```

will therefore forbid a plain team admin (or plain team owner) who is not also the organizer/attendee, which is a concrete logic bug introduced by using `&&` instead of `||` for the intended "admin OR owner" role.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:26-56 — no check of `booking.status`; guests can be added to cancelled/rejected bookings via direct API call (confidence=65, P2).

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuestsHandler`, the booking lookup only filters by `id` and the subsequent logic updates `booking.attendees` unconditionally once permission checks pass. There is no guard (e.g., `where: { id, status: ... }` or an explicit `if (booking.status === ...) throw`) preventing guest additions on non-active bookings (cancelled/rejected/etc.). This makes it possible to add guests to such bookings via the new `viewer.bookings.addGuests` mutation if the caller has access to the booking.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:92-106,145-146 — no seat-capacity enforcement or `BookingSeat` creation for `seatsPerTimeSlot`-enabled bookings (confidence=65, P2).

adjudication.rationale: The new `addGuestsHandler` simply appends new records to `booking.attendees` via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` and then updates calendars/emails. It does not reference `seatsPerTimeSlot` beyond copying it into the `CalendarEvent`, and it does not do any explicit capacity check. However, the finding’s core claim (that this must enforce seat capacity and/or create `BookingSeat` rows) depends on booking-seat semantics and the existence/usage of a `BookingSeat` model elsewhere, which is not shown in the diff. From the diff alone, it’s not verifiable that adding “guests” should consume seats or require `BookingSeat` creation rather than just adding attendees. Therefore this is largely speculative rather than a clearly demonstrated defect introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts + schema.ts — no recurring-event propagation ("apply to all remaining bookings"); adding a guest only affects the single instance with no UI/API acknowledgment (confidence=70, P2).

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an `addGuests` mutation that targets a single `bookingId` and updates only that booking’s `attendees` via `prisma.booking.update({ where: { id: bookingId }, ... })`. While the handler does include `recurringEvent: parseRecurringEvent(booking.eventType?.recurringEvent)` when building the CalendarEvent, there is no concept in the shown API/schema/UI of “apply to all remaining instances,” nor any indication that such propagation is required for correctness. Claiming this is a defect assumes product requirements about recurring bookings that are not present or implied by the diff; as written, “add guests to this booking instance” is a reasonable/consistent behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:74-78 — organizer's own email is never excluded from `guests`, so the organizer can be added as their own duplicate attendee (confidence=65, P2).

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the `uniqueGuests` array is computed by filtering out emails that already exist in `booking.attendees` and those in `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` (lines ~74-78). There is no check to exclude the booking organizer’s email (`organizer.email` or `booking.userPrimaryEmail`). Since the organizer is represented separately on the `CalendarEvent` (`evt.organizer`) and is not shown to be part of `booking.attendees` in this diff, the organizer can submit their own email in `guests` and it will pass the filter and be persisted via `attendees.createMany`, resulting in the organizer being added as an attendee as well. That’s a verifiable correctness issue in the introduced logic (at minimum it can create an unintended duplicate/extra attendee entry).

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:70-77 — case-sensitive blacklist/dedup comparison lets differently-cased duplicate/blacklisted emails through (confidence=55, P3).

Under concurrent addGuests requests for the same booking/emails, both requests can observe the same pre-update attendee list and both attempt to insert the same attendee emails, leading to duplicate rows (if no DB uniqueness constraint) or a write failure (if a uniqueness constraint exists).
